title: Plan 9 from Outer Space

evidence.note: Earlier research recorded a renewal at the US Copyright Office, RE0000279707, filed in 1986 by Wade Williams under the title 'Plan 9 from Outer Space'. We could not re-confirm that record in this session, because the Copyright Office catalog could not be searched automatically. Some commentators say the film is public domain because it was never renewed, and we found no court ruling or Copyright Office decision that settles the question. Whether any renewal is valid is a legal question we cannot verify, so this layer stays undetermined.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office Public Records System

evidence.note: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Parts 12-13: Motion Pictures and Filmstrips, Jan-Dec 1958 (archive.org identifier catalogofcopyrig3121213li). We confirmed the volume's title and year on its archive.org page, but we did not search its text for the film's entry in this session. The volume does not settle the renewal question, which depends on later Copyright Office records.
evidence.source: Internet Archive / Library of Congress Copyright Office

evidence.note: The recorded soundtrack as embodied in the film follows the film's own copyright status, which is undetermined (see the print layer). Individual musical compositions on the soundtrack may carry separate copyright histories, so check each composition before licensing it for new synchronization or commercial release.

The story is an original screenplay by Ed Wood and was not adapted from an earlier published work, so it takes the film's own status. That status is undetermined because of the renewal question described in the print layer.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office Public Records System

evidence.note: USPTO trademark databases could not be searched automatically in this session. We know of no active mark for 'Plan 9 from Outer Space', but trademark status remains undetermined until a USPTO search is completed.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: slavish reproduction of public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). Original additions such as a new score, colorization, or new titles and subtitles can be protected. Colorized versions of this film exist, and the colorization is protected on its own. Use archival prints rather than ripping a commercial disc, because ripping a copy-protected disc can implicate 17 U.S.C. § 1201.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp.

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. § 1201 — DMCA anti-circumvention prohibition on defeating technological protection measures.

editorial:
Ed Wood's American independent science-fiction horror film was produced by Reynolds Pictures, Inc. and shot in black and white in November 1956. It premiered on March 15, 1957 at the Carlton Theatre in Los Angeles under the working title Grave Robbers from Outer Space, then went into general release in July 1958 through Distributors Corporation of America. Ed Wood wrote and directed it. Bela Lugosi appears posthumously. The film is a staple of late-night TV and budget video, so many people assume it is free to use.

The rights trap is the renewal. Earlier research recorded a 1986 renewal, RE0000279707, filed by Wade Williams. We could not re-confirm it in this session. Some argue it is invalid, but we found no ruling that settles the point. Treat the film as possibly still protected and get advice before reusing it. Colorized versions add protected creative work of their own, whatever the status of the original black-and-white film.
faq: Can I use Plan 9 from Outer Space footage in my own film or video?

Not safely, as far as we can verify. Earlier research recorded a 1986 renewal (RE0000279707, filed by Wade Williams). Some argue it is invalid, but we found no ruling that settles it, so the film's status is undetermined. Get advice before reusing footage.
Is the colorized version of Plan 9 public domain too?

No. Colorization adds new creative authorship that is protected on its own, regardless of the original film's status. Even if the original black-and-white film is free to use, a colorized copy may not be.
